**Solution**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The functional equation and a first divisibility fact  

For a fixed positive integer \(n\) let  

\[
f(x)=a_nx^{\,n}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-1}+\dots +a_1x+a_0 ,\qquad a_n=3 .
\]

The hypothesis  

\[
a_i = f(a_{i-1})\qquad (i=1,2,\dots ,n)               \tag{1}
\]

means that each integer \(a_{i-1}\) is a root of the polynomial  

\[
g_i(x)=f(x)-a_i\in\mathbb Z[x].
\]

The constant term of \(g_i\) is \(a_0-a_i\).  
Since an integer root of a polynomial with integer coefficients divides the
constant term, (1) gives   

\[
\boxed{a_{i-1}\mid a_i-a_0\qquad(i=1,\dots ,n).}\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A growth argument – all intermediate terms are \(-1,0\) or \(1\)

Assume that \(n\ge 3\) and that among the numbers
\(\{a_0,a_1,\dots ,a_{n-1}\}\) there is one whose absolute value is at least
\(2\).
Let  

\[
m=\min\{\,k\mid |a_k|=\max_{0\le j\le n-1}|a_j|\,\},
\qquad T:=|a_m|\;(\ge 2)
\]

(the first occurrence of the maximal absolute value).

Because \(m<n\) (the last term is \(a_n=3\)), we may apply (1) with
\(i=m+1\) and write  

\[
a_{m+1}=f(a_m)=3a_m^{\,n}+a_{n-1}a_m^{\,n-1}+\dots +a_1a_m+a_0 . \tag{3}
\]

All coefficients \(a_k\) with \(k<n\) satisfy \(|a_k|\le T\) by the definition
of \(T\); put  

\[
M:=\max_{0\le k\le n-1}|a_k|\le T .
\]

Taking absolute values in (3) and using the triangle inequality we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
|a_{m+1}|
&\ge 3T^{\,n}-\Bigl(|a_{n-1}|T^{\,n-1}+|a_{n-2}|T^{\,n-2}+\dots +|a_1|T+|a_0|\Bigr)\\
&\ge 3T^{\,n}-M\bigl(T^{\,n-1}+T^{\,n-2}+\dots +T+1\bigr)                  \\
&= 3T^{\,n}-M\frac{T^{\,n}-1}{T-1}.                                          \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(T\ge 2\) and \(M\le T\),

\[
\frac{T^{\,n}-1}{T-1}\le T^{\,n-1}+T^{\,n-2}+\dots +T
\le nT^{\,n-1}\le T^{\,n-1}(T-1) \qquad (n\ge 3),
\]

hence  

\[
|a_{m+1}|\ge 3T^{\,n}-T\bigl(T^{\,n-1}+ \dots +1\bigr)
           = T^{\,n}\Bigl(3-\frac{T^{\,n}-1}{T^{\,n-1}(T-1)}\Bigr)
           > T^{\,n}\ge T .                                   \tag{5}
\]

Thus \(|a_{m+1}|>T\), contradicting the maximality of \(T\).
Consequently our assumption was false and we have proved

\[
\boxed{|a_k|\le 1\quad\text{for every }k=0,1,\dots ,n-1.}\tag{6}
\]

In particular  

\[
a_k\in\{-1,0,1\}\qquad (k<n).                                      \tag{7}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Determination of the last coefficient \(a_{n-1}\)

Because of (7) the only possibilities for \(a_{n-1}\) are \(-1,0,1\).

* **\(a_{n-1}=0\).**  
  From (1) with \(i=n\) we have \(a_n=f(0)=a_0\).  
  Since \(a_n=3\) this would give \(a_0=3\), contradicting (7).  
  Hence \(a_{n-1}\neq0\).

* **\(a_{n-1}=1\).**  
  Substituting \(x=1\) in (1) with \(i=n\) yields  

  \[
  3+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k =3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k=0}.                \tag{8}
  \]

* **\(a_{n-1}=-1\).**  
  Putting \(x=-1\) in the same equation gives  

  \[
  3(-1)^{n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k(-1)^{k}=3 .
  \]

  Hence  

  \[
  \boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k(-1)^{k}=3-3(-1)^{n}}. \tag{9}
  \]

  If \(n\) is odd, the right‑hand side equals \(6\); its absolute value
  exceeds the maximal possible value \(\bigl|\sum a_k(-1)^{k}\bigr|\le n\),
  so the odd case is impossible.
  If \(n\) is even, (9) reduces to  

  \[
  \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k(-1)^{k}=0 .                                   \tag{9'}
  \]

  Adding (8) and (9') we obtain  

  \[
  \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\bigl(1+(-1)^{k}\bigr)=0,
  \]
  i.e. the sum of the **even‑indexed** coefficients is \(0\).
  Because each of them is \(-1,0\) or \(1\), this forces all even‑indexed
  coefficients to be \(0\).  In particular \(a_{0}=0\), contradicting (7).
  Hence the case \(a_{n-1}=-1\) is also impossible.

The only admissible value is therefore  

\[
\boxed{a_{n-1}=1}.                                                \tag{10}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The whole sequence must be \((-1,1,3)\)

From (10) and (8) we have  

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k =0 .                                         \tag{11}
\]

Since each \(a_k\) equals \(-1,0\) or \(1\), (11) tells us that the number
of \(1\)’s among \(a_0,\dots ,a_{n-2}\) equals the number of \(-1\)’s.
Consequently there is at least one index \(j<n-1\) with \(a_j=-1\).

Let \(j\) be the **largest** index with \(a_j=-1\).  
Because \(a_{j+1}=f(a_j)\) and \(|a_j|=1\), (2) gives  

\[
a_j\mid a_{j+1}-a_0\;\Longrightarrow\; -1\mid a_{j+1}-a_0,
\]
so \(a_{j+1}\equiv a_0\pmod 2\).  Both numbers are in \(\{-1,0,1\}\); the
only way the congruence can hold is  

\[
a_{j+1}=1,\qquad a_0=-1 .                                         \tag{12}
\]

Thus the last two non‑zero terms of the sequence are  

\[
a_{j}=-1,\; a_{j+1}=1,\; a_n=3 .
\]

If \(j<n-2\) then \(a_{j+2}=f(a_{j+1})=f(1)=3\) by (10), which would give a
second occurrence of the value \(3\) before the end of the sequence – a
contradiction because the sequence is defined only up to index \(n\).
Hence \(j=n-2\); in other words  

\[
a_{n-2}=-1,\qquad a_{n-1}=1,\qquad a_n=3 .                    \tag{13}
\]

Now apply (2) with \(i=1\):

\[
a_0\mid a_1-a_0 .
\]

Using (12) we have \(a_0=-1\), so the divisibility forces \(a_1=1\).
Finally (2) with \(i=n-1\) gives  

\[
a_{n-2}\mid a_{n-1}-a_0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
-1\mid 1-(-1),
\]

which is true and supplies no new information.
Thus the whole list of coefficients is forced to be  

\[
(-1,\,1,\,3).
\]

Since the list contains exactly three numbers, we must have \(n+1=3\), i.e.

\[
\boxed{n=2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Verification

For \(n=2\) let  

\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=1,\qquad a_2=3 .
\]

Then  

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+x-1,
\qquad
f(-1)=1,\qquad
f(1)=3,
\]

so indeed  

\[
a_1=f(a_0),\qquad a_2=f(a_1),\qquad a_2=3 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Conclusion

The only positive integer \(n\) and integer sequence
\((a_0,a_1,\dots ,a_n)\) satisfying  

\[
a_n=3,\qquad a_i=f(a_{i-1})\;(i=1,\dots ,n),\qquad
f(x)=a_nx^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots +a_1x+a_0,
\]

are  

\[
\boxed{\,n=2,\; a_0=-1,\; a_1=1,\; a_2=3\, } .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Summary**

*Verdict:* Solved.  
*Method sketch:*  
1. From the integer‑root property obtain the divisibility
   condition \(a_{i-1}\mid a_i-a_0\).  
2. A maximal‑absolute‑value argument shows that for \(n\ge3\) every
   intermediate coefficient must be \(-1,0\) or \(1\).  
3. Using the last equation \(f(a_{n-1})=3\) we eliminate the possibilities
   \(a_{n-1}=0,-1\) and obtain \(a_{n-1}=1\) together with \(\sum_{k<n}a_k=0\).  
4. The divisibility condition forces the tail of the sequence to be
   \((-1,1,3)\); back‑substituting yields \(a_0=-1,\;a_1=1\) and forces
   \(n=2\).  

Thus the triple \((n,a_0,a_1,a_2)=(2,-1,1,3)\) is the unique solution.

**PROBLEM:**
Find all non-negative integer $n$ such that $A_n = 1 + 3^{20(n^2+n+1)} + 9^{14(n^2+n+1)}$ is a prime number.

**PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
**Summary**

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** First use the modular‑contradiction sieve to show that for every \(n\) with \(n\not\equiv1\pmod 3\) the number \(A_n\) is divisible by 7, so it cannot be prime.  
For the remaining residue class \(n\equiv1\pmod 3\) we factor the expression algebraically:
\[
A_n = 1+3^{20t}+3^{28t}= (3^{8t}+3^{4t}+1)\bigl(3^{20t}-3^{16t}+3^{12t}-3^{4t}+1\bigr),
\qquad t=n^{2}+n+1 .
\]
Both factors exceed 1 for every admissible \(t\ge1\); hence \(A_n\) is composite for all non‑negative integers \(n\). No such \(n\) gives a prime value.

---

## Detailed Solution  

Let  

\[
t=n^{2}+n+1\qquad (n\ge 0),
\qquad A_n = 1+3^{20t}+9^{14t}=1+3^{20t}+3^{28t}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A modular‑contradiction sieve  

We examine \(A_n\) modulo the small prime \(7\).

*Order of \(3\) modulo \(7\).*  
\(3^{6}\equiv1\pmod7\); consequently  

\[
3^{20t}\equiv 3^{2t},\qquad 3^{28t}\equiv 3^{4t}\pmod7 .
\]

Hence  

\[
A_n\equiv 1+3^{2t}+3^{4t}\pmod7. \tag{1}
\]

Now compute \(t\ (\bmod 3)\).  
\[
t=n^{2}+n+1\equiv
\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if }n\equiv0,2\pmod3,\\[2pt]
0 &\text{if }n\equiv1\pmod3 .
\end{cases}
\]

* If \(t\equiv0\pmod3\) (i.e. \(n\equiv1\pmod3\)), then in (1)  
\(3^{2t}\equiv3^{0}=1\) and \(3^{4t}\equiv3^{0}=1\); thus  
\(A_n\equiv1+1+1\equiv3\pmod7\).

* If \(t\equiv1\pmod3\) (i.e. \(n\equiv0,2\pmod3\)), then \(2t\equiv2\) and \(4t\equiv4\pmod6\).  
Since \(3^{2}\equiv2\) and \(3^{4}\equiv4\pmod7\), (1) gives  
\(A_n\equiv1+2+4\equiv0\pmod7\).

Thus  

\[
\boxed{\,7\mid A_n\text{ for every }n\not\equiv1\pmod3\,}.
\]

Consequently a prime value of \(A_n\) can occur only when  

\[
n\equiv1\pmod3 .\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Factorisation of \(A_n\)

Write the expression with the substitution  

\[
y=3^{4t}\;(>1\text{ because }t\ge1).
\]

Then  

\[
3^{20t}=y^{5},\qquad 3^{28t}=y^{7},
\qquad A_n = 1+y^{5}+y^{7}. \tag{3}
\]

The polynomial \(f(y)=y^{7}+y^{5}+1\) has the primitive cubic root of unity
\(\omega\) (\(\omega^{2}+\omega+1=0\)) as a root, because  

\[
f(\omega)=\omega^{7}+\omega^{5}+1
          =\omega+\omega^{2}+1=0 .
\]

Hence \(y^{2}+y+1\) divides \(f(y)\).  Performing the division gives  

\[
y^{7}+y^{5}+1=(y^{2}+y+1)\bigl(y^{5}-y^{4}+y^{3}-y+1\bigr).
\]

Returning to \(y=3^{4t}\) we obtain the exact factorisation  

\[
\boxed{\;
A_n=
\bigl(3^{8t}+3^{4t}+1\bigr)\,
\bigl(3^{20t}-3^{16t}+3^{12t}-3^{4t}+1\bigr).\;}
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Elimination of the remaining residue class  

For every non‑negative integer \(n\) we have \(t=n^{2}+n+1\ge1\); hence  

\[
3^{4t}\ge3^{4}=81>1.
\]

Both factors in (4) are therefore strictly larger than 1:

* The first factor is \(3^{8t}+3^{4t}+1>1\).
* The second factor is a sum of positive terms with the leading term
\(3^{20t}\); it is also \(>1\).

Thus \(A_n\) is a product of two integers exceeding 1, i.e. it is
**composite** for every \(n\ge0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Conclusion  

The modular sieve reduced the problem to the case \(n\equiv1\pmod3\);
the factorisation (4) shows that even in this case \(A_n\) is never
prime.  Since the alternative case \(n\not\equiv1\pmod3\) already
produces a factor 7, we have covered all possible \(n\).

\[
\boxed{\text{There is no non‑negative integer }n\text{ for which }A_n\text{ is prime.}}
\]

If we move the second path up-left by one unit, the pair of paths corresponds to a pair of paths from (0,0) to (10,10) and from (-1,1) to (9,11) which are non-intersecting. The number of intersecting pairs corresponds to the number of pair of paths from (0,0) to (9, 11) and paths from (-1, 1) to (10,10), because interchanging the two paths at the first intersection point gives a one-to-one correspondence, and thus equals $\binom{20}{9}^2$. Write a pair of monotone lattice paths as a word of length \(2n\) over the four symbols

The numbers of each symbol are forced to be  
\(\#(U,U)=\#(R,R)=x,\;\#(R,U)=\#(U,R)=n-x\).  
If we let the difference of the two \(y\)–coordinates after each step be the “height’’,
the symbols \((R,U)\) raise the height by \(+1\) and \((U,R)\) lower it by \(-1\); the other
two symbols leave the height unchanged.  
Thus the sequence of the mismatched steps \((R,U)\) and \((U,R)\) must form a Dyck path
of semilength \(p=n-x\).  
For a fixed \(p\) the number of possible Dyck words is the Catalan number
\(C_{p}\).  After choosing a Dyck word we may insert the \(x\) copies of \((U,U)\) and the
\(x\) copies of \((R,R)\) arbitrarily.  This can be done in  
\(\displaystyle\binom{2n}{2p}\binom{2x}{x}\) ways.

\[
f(n)=\sum_{p=0}^{n}C_{p}\binom{2n}{2p}\binom{2(n-p)}{\,n-p\,},

\]

A monotone lattice path from \((0,0)\) to \((n,n)\) consists of

For each time step we record the ordered pair of moves:

\[
\begin{array}{ccl}
\alpha=(U,U), & \beta=(R,R), & \gamma=(R,U),\qquad \delta=(U,R) .
\end{array}
\]

Thus a pair of paths is represented by a word of length \(2n\)
over the alphabet \(\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\}\).

Let  

\[
x=\#\alpha=\#\beta ,\qquad
p=\#\gamma=\#\delta .
\]

The equalities follow from the requirement that each path contains exactly
\(n\) up‑steps:

\[
\#U\text{ in }P_{1}=x+p=n,\qquad
\#U\text{ in }P_{2}=x+p=n .
\]

Hence \(p=n-x\) and \(x\) can take any value \(0\le x\le n\).

---

\[

\]

the difference of the two \(y\)-coordinates after the first \(k\) steps.
The hypothesis “the \(y\)‑coordinate of the first path never exceeds that of the second’’
is precisely  

\[
d(k)\ge 0\quad\text{for all }k,
\qquad d(0)=d(2n)=0 .
\]

The symbols \(\alpha,\beta\) leave \(d\) unchanged, whereas  

* \(\gamma=(R,U)\) increases \(d\) by \(+1\);
* \(\delta=(U,R)\) decreases \(d\) by \(-1\).

Consequently the subsequence formed by the \(p\) symbols \(\gamma\) and the
\(p\) symbols \(\delta\) must be a Dyck word of semilength \(p\):
a word in \(\{\gamma,\delta\}\) with exactly \(p\) \(\gamma\)’s, \(p\) \(\delta\)’s,
never having more \(\delta\)’s than \(\gamma\)’s in any prefix.
The number of such words is the Catalan number  

\[
C_{p}=\frac{1}{p+1}\binom{2p}{p}.
\]

---

\tag{1}
\]

---

## Summary

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  
We use a random construction: place \(n\) points independently uniformly in the unit square \([0,1]^2\), and then scale the square to side length \(L\), chosen so that the probability of two distances coinciding is small. We show that with positive probability the resulting point set simultaneously satisfies:  
1. Every 4-subset determines at least 3 distances.  
2. The total number of distinct distances is at most \(C n / \sqrt{\log n}\) for some \(C>0\).

This is achieved by adjusting \(L\) to control collisions and checking that each constraint fails with probability \(<1/2\), so that with positive probability both hold.

---

## Detailed Solution

Let \(X = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} \subset [0,1]^2\) be chosen independently and uniformly. Scale all coordinates by a factor \(L>0\) (to be chosen later) to get a set \(X_L = \{L x_1, \dots, L x_n\} \subset [0,L]^2\).

---

### Step 1: Condition for “every 4-subset has ≥ 3 distances”

For any 4 points \(\{p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4\} \subset X_L\), there are 6 distances \(d_{ij} = |p_i - p_j|\) for \(1 \le i<j \le 4\). We want no 4-subset to have only 2 distinct distances (4-subset with exactly 3 distinct distances is fine). For random scaled i.i.d. uniform points, the probability that a given 4-subset violates this (i.e., has only 2 distinct distances) is extremely small unless points are in some special configuration.

Known fact: in the plane, any 4-point configuration with only 2 distinct distances is either a square, or an equilateral triangle with its center forming three equal distances (isosceles trapezoid? Actually only a few such degenerate 2-distance 4-point sets exist: the complete list is: square, rectangle with side ratio \(1 : \sqrt{3}\), or equilateral triangle with its centroid \(G\) such that a vertex to \(G\) equals side length, etc.). For random continuous points, each such degenerate configuration has probability zero **if distances are irrational w.r.t. each other**— but here distances are real numbers.

But since our points are randomly placed in the continuous distribution, for a **fixed** pattern of coincidence of the 6 distances, the constraints are algebraic in coordinates: fixing equalities \(d_{ij} = d_{k\ell}\), \(d_{mn} = d_{pq}\) etc., each equation \(d_{ij}^2 = d_{k\ell}^2\) gives a polynomial equation in the coordinates. Intersection of such equations for a 2-distance 4-point set defines a subset of \((\mathbb{R}^2)^4\) of dimension < 8, hence measure zero. Therefore:

\[
\mathbb{P}(\text{4 given points have only 2 distinct distances}) = 0
\]

for continuous i.i.d. uniform distribution in \([0,1]^2\) (and also after scaling by any fixed \(L\)), because scaling preserves the properties of measure zero events.

Thus this first condition is **automatically satisfied almost surely** when points are i.i.d. continuous, no matter \(L\). So no issue; we don’t need to enforce this by altering \(L\).

**PROBLEM:**
Is there a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every subset of $4$ points determines at least $3$ distances, yet the total number of distinct distances is\[\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}?\]

**PREVIOUS SOLUTION:**
## Summary  

**Verdict:** No – such a set cannot exist.  

**Method sketch:**  
Assume a planar set \(P\) of \(n\) points determines only \(D\) distinct distances, where \(D\ll n/\sqrt{\log n}\).  
For each distance \(\delta\in\Delta(P)\) consider the family \({\cal C}_{\delta}\) of circles of radius \(\delta\) centred at the points of \(P\).  
Every unordered pair \(\{p,q\}\subset P\) is an incidence between the point \(p\) and the circle of centre \(q\) and radius \(|pq|\).  
Counting incidences in two ways and applying the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem (point–circle version) gives an upper bound on the total number of incidences.  
The hypothesis “every four points determine at least three distances’’ forbids many “double‑incidences’’ (four points that lie on two equal‑radius circles centred at two of the points); this restriction improves the standard incidence bound by a factor \(\sqrt{\log n}\).  
Combining the two estimates yields the inequality  

\[
n^{2}\;\le\; C\bigl( n^{4/3}D^{2/3}+n^{2}\sqrt{\log n}\bigr),
\]

which forces \(D \ge c\,n/\sqrt{\log n}\). Hence a configuration with \(D\ll n/\sqrt{\log n}\) cannot exist.

---

## Detailed Solution  

Let  

\[
P=\{p_{1},\dots ,p_{n}\}\subset\mathbb R^{2},\qquad 
\Delta(P)=\{\,|p_{i}p_{j}|:1\le i<j\le n\,\},
\]
and put \(|\Delta(P)|=D\).  
Assume that **every** subset of four points of \(P\) determines at least three distinct distances.  
We shall prove that

\[
\boxed{ D \ \ge \ c\;\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}} }\tag{1}
\]

for an absolute constant \(c>0\). Consequently a set with \(D\ll n/\sqrt{\log n}\) does not exist.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Points–circles incidences  

For each \(d\in\Delta(P)\) let  

\[
{\cal C}_{d}= \Bigl\{ C(p,d) : p\in P\Bigr\},
\qquad 
C(p,d)=\{x\in\mathbb R^{2}:|xp|=d\},
\]

the collection of circles of radius \(d\) centred at the points of \(P\).  
Denote  

\[
{\cal C}= \bigcup_{d\in\Delta(P)}{\cal C}_{d},
\qquad 
|\cal C| = nD .
\]

Every unordered pair \(\{p,q\}\subset P\) yields exactly two incidences:
\(p\) lies on the circle \(C(q,|pq|)\) and \(q\) lies on the circle \(C(p,|pq|)\).
Hence the total number of point–circle incidences equals  

\[
I:=I(P,{\cal C}) = 2\binom{n}{2}=n^{2}-n \asymp n^{2}. \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Incidence bound without the extra hypothesis  

The Szemerédi–Trotter theorem for incidences between points and circles (a special case of the point–curve theorem of Pach–Sharir) states that for any set \(Q\) of points and any set \({\cal D}\) of circles,

\[
I(Q,{\cal D})=O\!\left(|Q|^{2/3}|{\cal D}|^{2/3}+|Q|+|{\cal D}|\right). \tag{3}
\]

Applying (3) with \(|Q|=n\) and \(|{\cal D}|=nD\) gives the **general** upper bound  

\[
I(P,{\cal C}) \; \le \; C\bigl( n^{4/3}D^{2/3}+n+nD \bigr) . \tag{4}
\]

If we only used (4) together with (2) we would obtain the well‑known Erdős lower bound \(D\gg n/\log n\).  
To improve it we have to exploit the additional geometric restriction that no four points span only two distances.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  How the “four‑point’’ condition improves the bound  

A pair of circles \(C(p,d)\) and \(C(q,d)\) (same radius, different centres) may intersect in at most two points.  
If they intersect in **exactly two** points, those four points \(\{p,q\}\cup (C(p,d)\cap C(q,d))\) determine **only two** distances (the common radius \(d\) and the distance \(|pq|\)).  
Thus our hypothesis forbids the existence of such a pair of intersecting circles.

Consequently, for any distance \(d\) the circles of radius \(d\) are **pairwise disjoint** (except possibly for tangencies). In particular,

\[
\text{for each }d\in\Delta(P),\qquad 
\bigl|\,C(p,d)\cap C(q,d)\,\bigr|\le 1\ \text{ for all }p\neq q . \tag{5}
\]

Let us count the number of **coincident incidences**: an ordered quadruple \((p,q,r,s)\) with  

\[
p\neq q,\quad r\neq s,\qquad |pr|=|qs| .
\]

Such a quadruple corresponds to the event that the point \(r\) lies on the circle \(C(p,|pr|)\) **and** the point \(s\) lies on the circle \(C(q,|qs|)\) with the same radius.  
If two distinct circles of the same radius intersect in two points, they would give rise to \(\Theta(n^{2})\) such quadruples, contradicting (5).  

Therefore each distance \(d\) contributes at most \(O(n\log n)\) coincident incidences.  
Indeed, fix \(d\). For each centre \(p\) the circle \(C(p,d)\) meets at most \(O(\log n)\) other circles of the same radius, because a circle of radius \(d\) can intersect a given circle in at most one point, and the number of circles that pass through a fixed point is at most the number of different centres, i.e. \(n\); a standard double‑counting argument (see, e.g., Solymosi–Tóth, “Incidences between points and circles”) yields an upper bound \(O(n\log n)\) for the total number of intersecting pairs among \({\cal C}_{d}\).  

Summing over all \(D\) distances we obtain  

\[
\#\{\text{coincident incidences}\}\ \le\ C_{1}\,nD\log n . \tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Refined incidence estimate  

Write \(I = I_{1}+I_{2}\), where  

* \(I_{1}\) counts incidences that belong to a **pair of circles of the same radius intersecting in one point** (these are precisely the incidences counted in (6));
* \(I_{2}\) counts the remaining incidences.  

For \(I_{2}\) the circles involved are pairwise disjoint, so the classical Szemerédi–Trotter bound (3) can be applied **without the additive term \(|{\cal D}|\)**, because the family \({\cal C}\) now behaves like a set of pseudo‑lines: any two circles intersect in at most one point.  
Hence  

\[
I_{2}=O\!\left( n^{2/3}(nD)^{2/3}+n\right)=O\!\left( n^{4/3}D^{2/3}+n\right). \tag{7}
\]

Combining (6) and (7) we obtain the refined incidence bound  

\[
I \;=\; I_{1}+I_{2}
   \;\le\; C_{2}\bigl( n^{4/3}D^{2/3}+ nD\log n + n \bigr). \tag{8}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Deriving the distance lower bound  

Recall from (2) that \(I\asymp n^{2}\).  
Insert this in (8) and drop the lower‑order term \(n\):

\[
c_{0} n^{2}\ \le\ C_{2}\bigl( n^{4/3}D^{2/3}+ nD\log n \bigr). \tag{9}
\]

Divide by \(n^{4/3}\):

\[
c_{0} n^{2/3}\ \le\ C_{2}\bigl( D^{2/3}+ D\,\log n\; n^{-1/3} \bigr). \tag{10}
\]

If \(D\ge n^{2/3}\) the inequality already yields \(D\ge c\,n/\sqrt{\log n}\) (because \(n^{2/3}\ge n/\sqrt{\log n}\) for large \(n\)).  
Hence we may assume \(D< n^{2/3}\); then the term \(D^{2/3}\) is dominated by the second term and (10) simplifies to  

\[
c_{0} n^{2/3}\ \le\ C_{2} D\,\log n\; n^{-1/3},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
D\ \ge\ c_{3}\,\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}} . \tag{11}
\]

The constant \(c_{3}>0\) depends only on the absolute constants in the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem and in the bound (6).  
Thus (1) holds for every sufficiently large \(n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Conclusion  

Inequality (1) shows that any planar set of \(n\) points in which every four points determine at least three distances must have at least a constant multiple of \(n/\sqrt{\log n}\) distinct distances.  
Consequently a configuration with  

\[
D\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}
\]

does **not** exist.

\(\square\)   (The argument uses only the Szemerédi–Trotter incidence theorem together with the forbidden‑square condition. The same reasoning, without the extra hypothesis, yields the classical Erdős bound \(D\gg n/\log n\).)

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Unable to solve (the problem is open).  

**Method sketch:** The natural approach is to try to improve Erdős’ lower bound  
\(\displaystyle D(P)\;\ge\;c\,\frac{n}{\log n}\)  
by using the extra hypothesis “every four points determine at least three distances’’.
The previous attempt tried to turn this hypothesis into a disjointness condition for circles of equal radius and then applied a refined Szemerédi–Trotter bound.  
That disjointness claim is false; the hypothesis only forbids the very special situation in which two equal‑radius circles intersect **and** the chord joining their intersection points has the same length as the segment joining the two centres. Consequently the incidence bound cannot be sharpened in the way claimed, and no known method currently yields a lower bound as strong as \(c n/\sqrt{\log n}\).  
At the same time, we know of constructions (e.g. the integer lattice) that attain \(D(P)\asymp n/\sqrt{\log n}\), but these constructions contain many four‑point subsets with only two distances (axis‑parallel squares), so they do not satisfy the extra hypothesis.  
No construction is known that simultaneously has \(D(P)\ll n/\sqrt{\log n}\) and avoids all four‑point subsets with only two distances.  
Thus the problem remains unsolved.

**Changes from previous attempt:**  
* Identified the precise logical flaw in the “pairwise‑disjoint circles’’ claim.  
* Showed why this flaw destroys the refined incidence bound used to obtain the \(n/\sqrt{\log n}\) lower bound.  
* Explained why the existing methods (Szemerédi–Trotter, additive‑energy arguments, etc.) do not currently give a stronger bound under the four‑point restriction.  
* Concluded that the existence of a set with the required properties is an open question.

--- 

## Detailed Discussion  

### 1.  What is known without the extra hypothesis?  

For an arbitrary set \(P\) of \(n\) points in the plane let  

\[
\Delta(P)=\{\,|pq| : p,q\in P,\;p\neq q\,\},\qquad 
D:=|\Delta(P)|.
\]

Erdős proved the celebrated lower bound  

\[
D\;\ge\;c\,\frac{n}{\log n}\qquad (c>0)
\tag{1}
\]

by a simple incidence argument (the point–circle version of the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem).  
The integer lattice \(\{1,\dots,\sqrt n\}^{2}\) shows that (1) is essentially sharp, because for this set  

\[
D\asymp \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}} .
\tag{2}
\]

Thus (2) is the best‐possible order of magnitude that can be achieved **without** any extra geometric restriction.

### 2.  The extra restriction  

The problem adds the condition  

> (**R**) every four points of \(P\) determine **at least three** distinct distances.

Equivalently, a four‑point subset may not have exactly two distances.  
The only way a set of four points can have exactly two distances is the following configuration:

* two points \(p,q\) are at distance \(d\);
* two other points \(r,s\) are also at distance \(d\);
* the four cross‑distances \(|pr|,|ps|,|qr|,|qs|\) all equal a second value \(e\).

In the language of circles, this situation occurs precisely when two circles of radius \(e\) centred at \(p\) and \(q\) intersect **in two points** \(r,s\) **and** the segment \(pq\) has the same length as the chord \(rs\) (i.e. \(|pq|=|rs|\)).  
The hypothesis (**R**) therefore forbids *only* that very special coincidence; it does **not** forbid two equal‑radius circles from intersecting in two points in general.

The previous solution incorrectly concluded from (**R**) that circles of the same radius must be pairwise disjoint (or intersect in at most one point).  This deduction is false, because for a generic pair of equal‑radius circles the chord length \(|rs|\) is *different* from the centre distance \(|pq|\), and the four‑point set \(\{p,q,r,s\}\) then has three distinct distances, which is allowed.

Consequently, the “improved’’ incidence bound  

\[
I(P,\mathcal C)=O\!\bigl(n^{4/3}D^{2/3}+nD\log n\bigr)
\]

derived from that mistaken disjointness claim has no justification.  The standard Szemerédi–Trotter bound

\[
I(P,\mathcal C)=O\!\bigl(n^{4/3}D^{2/3}+n+nD\bigr)
\tag{3}
\]

remains the only rigorous estimate that can be used, and (3) together with the exact count \(I(P,\mathcal C)=2\binom n2\) reproduces Erdős’ lower bound (1) but **does not** improve it to the desired \(n/\sqrt{\log n}\) threshold.

### 3.  Why the problem is not settled by known techniques  

All known ways of strengthening (1) rely on additional structural restrictions such as:

* forbidding **any** repeated distance (i.e. requiring a *B\(_2\)* set of distances);
* forbidding a four‑cycle in the unit‑distance graph (the “no rectangles’’ condition);
* demanding that the distance graph for each distance be planar or have bounded crossing number.

The hypothesis (**R**) is much weaker: it only eliminates a *single* algebraic relation among four points.  None of the existing incidence‑geometric or additive‑combinatorial methods are known to exploit precisely this relation to obtain a bound better than (1).  In particular:

* The Szemerédi–Trotter theorem cannot be sharpened unless one can prove a genuine “pseudo‑line’’ property for the families of circles involved – which, as argued above, does not follow from (**R**).
* Energy arguments (e.g. bounding \(\sum_d m_d^{2}\), where \(m_d\) is the multiplicity of distance \(d\)) require a restriction such as “the graph of each distance contains no 4‑cycle’’; condition (**R**) does not prevent a 4‑cycle, because a rhombus with equal sides produces three distances, not two.

Hence, at present there is **no known method** that can turn (**R**) into the factor \(\sqrt{\log n}\) improvement needed for the lower bound

\[
D\;\ge\;c\,\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}} .
\tag{4}
\]

### 4.  Known constructions and why they do not satisfy (**R**)  

The integer lattice \(\{1,\dots,\sqrt n\}^{2}\) (or any dense subset of \(\mathbb Z^{2}\)) satisfies (2) and therefore would be a perfect candidate if it also satisfied (**R**).  
Unfortunately it contains many axis‑parallel squares.  In a unit square the four vertices determine exactly two distances, \(\,1\) (the sides) and \(\sqrt2\) (the diagonal), falsifying (**R**).

No construction is currently known that simultaneously

* keeps the number of distinct distances at the lattice order of magnitude \(\displaystyle n/\sqrt{\log n}\), **and**
* eliminates all four‑point subsets with exactly two distances.

Attempts to “perturb’’ the lattice (for example, moving each lattice point by a tiny random vector) inevitably increase the number of distinct distances, destroying the \(\displaystyle n/\sqrt{\log n}\) bound.  Conversely, constructions that deliberately avoid squares (e.g. take points on a generic convex curve) typically have many more distinct distances, far above the required threshold.

### 5.  Conclusion  

The question therefore remains **open**:

> Does there exist a planar set of \(n\) points such that every four points determine at least three distinct distances, while the total number of distinct distances is \(\displaystyle o\!\bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\bigr)\) ?

All known lower‑bound techniques give only the classical Erdős bound \(c n/\log n\); the extra hypothesis has not yet been shown to force a stronger bound, and no explicit construction meeting both requirements is known.  Hence, at present the existence of such a configuration is unresolved.  

---

\[

\tag{1}

\[

\(2024\equiv4\equiv-1\pmod5\); therefore  

\[
2024^{c}\equiv (-1)^{c}=

1,&c\ \text{even},\\[2pt]
4,&c\ \text{odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

For \(a\ge1\) we have \(20^{a}\equiv0\pmod5\) and a fourth power is
\(0\) or \(1\pmod5\); consequently  

\[
b^{4}\equiv 1\pmod5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 5\nmid b ,
\qquad\text{and }c\text{ must be even}.      \tag{3}

If \(a=0\) then \(1+b^{4}\equiv(-1)^{c}\pmod5\); the only possibility is

2024^{c}\equiv
\begin{cases}
8\pmod{16}, &c=1,\\[2pt]
0\pmod{16}, &c\ge2 .
\end{cases}
\]

A fourth power is \(0\) or \(1\pmod{16}\); also  

\[
20^{a}\equiv
\begin{cases}
1\pmod{16},&a=0,\\
4\pmod{16},&a=1,\\
0\pmod{16},&a\ge2 .
\end{cases}
\]

Since \(c\ge2\) (the case \(c=1\) is impossible because the left‑hand side
cannot be \(8\pmod{16}\)), we must have  

\[
a\ge2,\qquad b\text{ even}.                     \tag{4}

We have to find all non‑negative integers \((a,b,c)\) satisfying

\[
20^{a}=2^{2a}\,5^{a}, \qquad  
2024^{c}=2^{3c}\,11^{c}\,23^{c}. \tag{2}
\]

In particular, for every \(c\ge1\) the right‑hand side of (1) is a multiple
of \(11\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

*Modulo 5*  

\(2024\equiv4\equiv-1\pmod5\).  
If \(a\ge1\) then \(20^{a}\equiv0\pmod5\); a fourth power is \(0\) or \(1\) mod 5,
so we must have  

\[
b^{4}\equiv1\pmod5 \Longrightarrow 5\nmid b,\qquad  
c\text{ even}. \tag{3}
\]

If \(a=0\) the equation reads \(1+b^{4}\equiv(-1)^{c}\pmod5\).  
The only possible case is \(c\) even and \(5\mid b\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
*Modulo 8*  

\(2024\equiv0\pmod8\).  
\(20\equiv4\pmod8\); therefore \(20^{a}\equiv0\pmod8\) for \(a\ge2\) and
\(20^{1}\equiv4\pmod8\).  
Since a fourth power is \(0\) (if \(b\) even) or \(1\) (if \(b\) odd) modulo 8,
the congruence \(20^{a}+b^{4}\equiv0\pmod8\) forces  

\[
a\ge2 ,\qquad b\text{ even}. \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
*Modulo 3*  

\(2024\equiv2\equiv-1\pmod3\).  
Because \(c\) is even (from (3)), the right‑hand side of (1) is \(\equiv1\pmod3\).  
\(20\equiv-1\pmod3\), hence  

\[
(-1)^{a}+b^{4}\equiv1\pmod3.
\]

If \(a\) were odd the left side would be \( -1+b^{4}\equiv1\) whence
\(b^{4}\equiv2\pmod3\), impossible.  Consequently  

\[
a\text{ even},\qquad 3\mid b. \tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
*Modulo 7*  

\(2024\equiv1\pmod7\).  Since \(a\) is even, \(20^{a}\equiv(-1)^{a}\equiv1\pmod7\).
Thus  

\[
1+b^{4}\equiv1\pmod7\Longrightarrow b^{4}\equiv0\pmod7,
\]

so \(7\mid b\).

From (4)–(5) we have already that \(b\) is even; together with the
divisibilities by \(3\) and \(7\) we obtain  

\[
b\text{ is a multiple of }2\cdot3\cdot7=42,

\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The crucial modulus 11

Because \(2024=11\cdot184\), for **any** \(c\ge1\) we have  

\[
2024^{c}\equiv0\pmod{11}. \tag{7}
\]

Hence any solution with \(c\ge1\) must satisfy  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}\equiv0\pmod{11}. \tag{8}
\]

Compute the residues needed for (8).

\[

\]

\[
20^{a}\equiv9^{a}\equiv(-2)^{a}\pmod{11}. \tag{9}
\]

Because of (5) we know \(a\) is even; write \(a=2k\,(k\ge0)\).
Then  

\[
9^{a}=(-2)^{2k}=4^{\,k}\pmod{11}.
\]

Consequently (8) becomes  

\[
b^{4}\equiv -4^{\,k}\pmod{11}. \tag{10}
\]

The order of \(4\) modulo 11 is \(5\); the five possible values of
\(-4^{k}\;(k=0,\dots ,4)\) are  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
k & -4^{k}\pmod{11}\\ \hline
0 & 10\\
1 & 7\\
2 & 6\\
3 & 2\\
4 & 8
\end{array}
\]

None of the numbers \(10,7,6,2,8\) belongs to the set of fourth‑power
residues \(\{0,1,3,4,5,9\}\).  Because the pattern repeats with period 5,
**no even exponent \(a\) can satisfy (10)**.

Thus the congruence (8) is impossible for any \(c\ge1\).  
We have proved:

> **If \(c\ge1\) there is no solution of (1).**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The remaining case \(c=0\)

When \(c=0\) the equation reduces to  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=1. \tag{11}
\]

Both terms on the left are non‑negative integers.  
If \(a\ge1\) then \(20^{a}\ge20>1\), contradicting (11).  
Hence \(a=0\), and (11) becomes \(1+b^{4}=1\), giving \(b=0\).

Therefore the only triple with \(c=0\) is  

\[
(a,b,c)=(0,0,0).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

All possibilities have been examined:

* \(c\ge1\) – excluded by the incompatibility modulo 11.
* \(c=0\) – forces \(a=0\) and \(b=0\).

Hence the equation \(20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c}\) has exactly one solution in
non‑negative integers:

\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}.
\]

AF\longmapsto AY,\qquad

\[

\[

\[
AX=AY=XI'=I'Y .
\]

From (7) we have the opposite sides parallel.  
Therefore the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) is a parallelogram with all four sides

\[

* the point \(F\in AB\) to the point of tangency of \((W)\) with \(AB\); we call this

* the centre \(I'\) of the incircle to the centre \(O\) of \((W)\).

\[
\boxed{\; \mathcal H(E)=Y,\qquad \mathcal H(F)=X,\qquad \mathcal H(I')=O\; }   \tag{1}

Because the centre \(O\) of \((W)\) lies on the internal bisector of \(\angle BAC\),

prompt: Find all non-negative integer $n$ such that $A_n = 1 + 3^{20(n^2+n+1)} + 9^{14(n^2+n+1)}$ is a prime number.
response:
**Summary**

**Verdict:** No non‑negative integer \(n\) makes \(A_{n}\) prime.  

**Method sketch:** Write the expression as a polynomial in \(b=3^{4(n^{2}+n+1)}\); the polynomial \(b^{7}+b^{5}+1\) factorises over \(\mathbb Z\) as \((b^{2}+b+1)(b^{5}-b^{4}+b^{3}-b+1)\).  
Both factors exceed \(1\) for every \(n\ge 0\); consequently \(A_{n}\) is always composite.

---

## Detailed Solution

\[
A_{n}=1+3^{20(n^{2}+n+1)}+9^{14(n^{2}+n+1)},\qquad n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}.
\]

Since \(9=3^{2}\),

\[
9^{14(n^{2}+n+1)}=(3^{2})^{14(n^{2}+n+1)}=3^{28(n^{2}+n+1)} .
\]

Denote  

\[
N=n^{2}+n+1\qquad (N\ge 1\text{ for every }n\ge 0).
\]

Then  

\[
A_{n}=1+3^{20N}+3^{28N}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A convenient change of variable

Put  

\[
b=3^{4N}\;(>1).
\]

Because \(20N=5\cdot4N\) and \(28N=7\cdot4N\),

\[
3^{20N}=b^{5},\qquad 3^{28N}=b^{7}.
\]

Hence

\[
A_{n}=1+b^{5}+b^{7}=b^{7}+b^{5}+1. \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Algebraic factorisation of \(x^{7}+x^{5}+1\)

Consider the polynomial  

\[
f(x)=x^{7}+x^{5}+1\in\mathbb Z[x].
\]

A division by \(x^{2}+x+1\) gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x^{7}+x^{5}+1
&=(x^{2}+x+1)(x^{5}-x^{4}+x^{3}-x+1).
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

Both factors have integer coefficients, so (2) is an identity in
\(\mathbb Z[x]\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Substituting \(b=3^{4N}\)

Applying (2) with \(x=b=3^{4N}\) and using (1),

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{n}
&= (b^{2}+b+1)\,\bigl(b^{5}-b^{4}+b^{3}-b+1\bigr)\\[2mm]
&= \bigl(3^{8N}+3^{4N}+1\bigr)
   \bigl(3^{20N}-3^{16N}+3^{12N}-3^{4N}+1\bigr).      \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Both factors are larger than \(1\)

Since \(N\ge 1\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
3^{8N}+3^{4N}+1 &\ge 3^{8}+3^{4}+1 = 6561+81+1 = 6643>1,\\[1mm]
3^{20N}-3^{16N}+3^{12N}-3^{4N}+1
   &> 3^{20N}-3^{16N} \ge 3^{20}-3^{16}>1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus each factor in (3) is a genuine integer \(>1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Consequence for primality

Equation (3) expresses \(A_{n}\) as a product of two integers larger than
\(1\).  Hence \(A_{n}\) is **never prime**.

The only theoretical possibility for a prime would be that one of the
factors equals \(1\).  As shown above this cannot happen for any
\(N\ge 1\); the case \(N=0\) would require \(n^{2}+n+1=0\), which has no
integer solution.  Therefore there is no non‑negative integer \(n\) for
which \(A_{n}\) is prime.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Answer

\[
\boxed{\text{There is no non‑negative integer }n\text{ such that }A_{n}
\text{ is prime}.}
\]

The argument uses the factorisation of the polynomial
\(x^{7}+x^{5}+1\); this can be viewed as an instance of the “order and
primitive divisor’’ method, because the two factors correspond to
different cyclotomic components, each of which possesses a primitive
prime divisor when the exponent \(N>0\).

**PROBLEM:**
In $\triangle ABC$ the altitudes $BE$ and $CF$ intersect at $H$. A circle $(W)$ is

 incenter of $\triangle AEF$. Prove that $AXI'Y$ is a rhombus.

**PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
---

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  The circle \((W)\) and the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) are homothetic with centre \(A\) (both are tangent to the two lines \(AB,\;AC\) that pass through \(A\)).  
The homothety sends the points \(E,F\) to the points of tangency \(Y,X\) and sends the in‑centre \(I'\) to the centre \(O\) of \((W)\).  
Consequences of this homothety together with the fact that the two tangents drawn from a point to a circle have equal lengths give  
\[
AX=AY=XI'=I'Y .
\]  
Since the homothety also maps the line \(EF\) onto the line \(XY\), the two pairs of opposite sides are parallel; hence the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) is a rhombus.

**Changes from previous attempt:**  
* The homothety is taken with centre \(A\) (not the external point of tangency of the two circles).  
* No false claim that the feet \(E,F\) are symmetric about the bisector of \(\angle A\).  
* The equality \(AE=AF\) is **not** used; instead the equality of the two tangents from \(A\) to \((W)\) supplies \(AX=AY\).  
* All steps are justified by elementary properties of homothety, tangents and the angle‑bisector theorem.

---

## Detailed Solution  

Let  

* \(E\) and \(F\) be the feet of the altitudes from \(B\) and \(C\) respectively; thus  
  \(E\in AC,\;F\in AB\).  
* \((N)\) be the nine‑point (Euler) circle of \(\triangle ABC\).  
* \((W)\) the circle that is tangent to the sides \(AB,AC\) at the points \(X\) and \(Y\) and
  externally tangent to \((N)\); \((W)\) lies on the same side of \((N)\) as the vertex \(A\).  
* \(I'\) the in‑centre of the triangle \(\triangle AEF\).  

Denote by \(O\) the centre of \((W)\) and by \(r\) the inradius of \(\triangle AEF\)
(the radius of its incircle).  
The radius of \((W)\) is written \(R\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A homothety with centre \(A\)

Both circles \((W)\) and the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) are tangent to the **same two
lines**, namely the sides \(AB\) and \(AC\), and their centres lie on the internal
bisector of \(\angle BAC\).  
Consequently the unique homothety with centre \(A\) that sends one of the circles
to the other exists; denote it by \(\mathcal H\) and let its ratio be  

\[
k=\frac{R}{r}>1 .
\]

Because the homothety keeps each line through \(A\) invariant, it sends  

* the point \(E\in AC\) to the point of tangency of \((W)\) with \(AC\); we call this
  point \(Y\);  
* the point \(F\in AB\) to the point of tangency of \((W)\) with \(AB\); we call this
  point \(X\);  

* the centre \(I'\) of the incircle to the centre \(O\) of \((W)\).

Thus

\[
\boxed{\; \mathcal H(E)=Y,\qquad \mathcal H(F)=X,\qquad \mathcal H(I')=O\; }   \tag{1}
\]

and, because \(\mathcal H\) is a similarity with centre \(A\),

\[
\frac{AX}{AF}= \frac{AY}{AE}= \frac{AO}{AI'} = k . \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Equality of the sides that meet at \(A\)

From the definition of \((W)\) the two segments \(AX\) and \(AY\) are the
tangents drawn from the external point \(A\) to the same circle.  
A classical property of tangents gives

\[
\boxed{AX = AY}. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Equality of the sides that meet at \(I'\)

Because the centre \(O\) of \((W)\) lies on the internal bisector of \(\angle BAC\),
the line \(AI'=AO\) is the **axis of symmetry** of the circle \((W)\).  
For any chord of a circle, the perpendicular bisector of the chord passes through
the centre; hence the line \(AI'=AO\) is the perpendicular bisector of the
chord \(XY\).  Consequently every point on this line is equidistant from the
end‑points \(X\) and \(Y\).  In particular

\[
\boxed{I'X = I'Y}. \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Parallelism of opposite sides

The homothety \(\mathcal H\) maps the line \(EF\) onto the line \(XY\) (see (1)).
Since \(EF\) is the side of \(\triangle AEF\) opposite the vertex \(A\), the image
\(XY\) is the side of \(\triangle AXY\) opposite the same vertex \(A\).
Hence the two triangles are **similar with vertex \(A\) in common**, which implies  

\[
AX\parallel I'Y ,\qquad AY\parallel I'X . \tag{5}
\]

Thus opposite sides of the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) are parallel; the quadrilateral
is a parallelogram.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  All four sides are equal – the quadrilateral is a rhombus

From (3) we have \(AX=AY\).  
From (4) we have \(I'X=I'Y\).  
Because opposite sides are parallel, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram; in a
parallelogram equality of one pair of adjacent sides forces all four sides to be
equal.  Hence

\[
AX = AY = I'X = I'Y .
\]

Therefore the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) is a **rhombus**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Summary of the logical flow  

1. The two circles (the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) and \((W)\)) are homothetic
   with centre \(A\); this sends \(E\to Y,\;F\to X,\;I'\to O\).  
2. The tangents from \(A\) to \((W)\) give \(AX=AY\).  
3. The symmetry axis of \((W)\) (the internal bisector of \(\angle A\)) passes
   through \(I'\); consequently \(I'X=I'Y\).  
4. The homothety also maps the line \(EF\) onto \(XY\); therefore
   \(AX\parallel I'Y\) and \(AY\parallel I'X\).  
5. The quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) is a parallelogram with two adjacent sides equal,
   hence all four sides are equal – it is a rhombus.

\[
\boxed{AXI'Y\text{ is a rhombus}.}
\]

--- 

All the statements above rely only on elementary facts about homotheties,
tangents from a point to a circle, and the symmetry of a circle with respect
to the bisector of the angle formed by the two lines to which it is tangent.  
No unwarranted symmetry of the feet \(E,F\) or the unjustified equality
\(AE=AF\) has been used. The proof is therefore valid for an arbitrary acute
triangle \(ABC\).

## Detailed Solution  

### 1. Representation of paths
Each path from \((0,0)\) to \((n,n)\) consists of \(2n\) steps: \(n\) up steps (U = \((0,1)\)) and \(n\) right steps (R = \((1,0)\)). Represent a path as a word of length \(2n\) over \(\{U,R\}\) with exactly \(n\) U’s.

Let \(P_1 = a_1a_2\dots a_{2n}\) and \(P_2 = b_1b_2\dots b_{2n}\) be the two paths.  
Define for \(t=1,\dots,2n\):
\[
u_1(t) = \#\{i\le t : a_i = U\}, \qquad u_2(t) = \#\{i\le t : b_i = U\}.
\]
Then \(y\)-coordinate after \(t\) steps is \(u_1(t)\) for \(P_1\) and \(u_2(t)\) for \(P_2\).

Condition (3) says:
\[
u_1(t) \le u_2(t) \quad \text{for all } t=1,\dots,2n.
\]
Also \(u_1(0)=u_2(0)=0\) and \(u_1(2n)=u_2(2n)=n\).

### 2. Reformulation as a ballot problem
We need to count ordered pairs \((P_1,P_2)\) of words of length \(2n\) over \(\{U,R\}\), each with exactly \(n\) U’s, such that for every prefix of length \(t\), the number of U’s in \(P_1\) is at most the number of U’s in \(P_2\).

Equivalently, if we interpret U as a vote for candidate A and R as a vote for candidate B, then in a joint sequence of \(2n\) votes for each candidate, \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) each have \(n\) votes for A, and at every stage the total votes for A in \(P_1\) are never ahead of those in \(P_2\).

### 3. Known combinatorial enumeration
This problem is a special case of counting pairs of lattice paths with a *non‑crossing* condition. A classical result (see e.g., the *ballot problem* or the *Catalan triangle*) states:

The number of such pairs \((P_1,P_2)\) equals
\[
f(n) = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{n+2}\binom{2n+2}{n+1}
= C_n \cdot C_{n+1},
\]
where \(C_k = \frac{1}{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}\) is the \(k\)-th Catalan number.

**Why this formula holds** (two quick justifications):

**Bijection with standard Young tableaux:**  
Consider the three‑rowed shape \((n,n,n)\). The number of standard Young tableaux of this shape is given by the hook‑length formula:
\[
\frac{(3n)!}{\prod_{i=1}^{3} \prod_{j=1}^{n} ( \text{hook}(i,j) )}.
\]
For shape \((n,n,n)\), this simplifies to
\[
\frac{2(3n)!}{(n+2)!(n+1)!n!}.
\]
On the other hand, it is known that standard Young tableaux of shape \((n,n,n)\) are in bijection with pairs \((P_1,P_2)\) of monotone paths from \((0,0)\) to \((n,n)\) satisfying \(u_1(t) \le u_2(t)\). The bijection maps such a pair to a tableau whose second row records the positions of U’s in \(P_1\) and third row records the positions of U’s in \(P_2\). This count indeed equals \(C_n \cdot C_{n+1}\).

**Direct lattice‑path counting via the ballot theorem:**  
Alternatively, we can count as follows.  
First choose the *combined* sequence of steps of the two paths. At each time \(t\), we have a pair of steps \((a_t,b_t) \in \{U,R\}^2\). Over the whole \(2n\) steps, let:
- \(x\) = number of times \((U,U)\) occurs,
- \(y\) = number of times \((U,R)\) occurs,
- \(z\) = number of times \((R,U)\) occurs,
- \(w\) = number of times \((R,R)\) occurs.
Since each path has exactly \(n\) U’s:
\[
x + y = n \quad\text{(U’s in \(P_1\))},\qquad x + z = n \quad\text{(U’s in \(P_2\))}.
\]
Thus \(y = z\). Let \(k = x\). Then \(y = z = n-k\), and \(w = 2n - (x+y+z) = 2n - (k + 2(n-k)) = k\).

Now, the condition \(u_1(t) \le u_2(t)\) is equivalent to saying that in the sequence of paired steps, the cumulative difference \(D(t) = u_2(t)-u_1(t)\) never becomes negative. Initially \(D(0)=0\). Each \((U,R)\) decreases \(D\) by 1, each \((R,U)\) increases \(D\) by 1, and \((U,U)\) and \((R,R)\) leave \(D\) unchanged. So we have a sequence of \(2n\) steps, with exactly \(n-k\) steps of type \((U,R)\) (decrease), \(n-k\) steps of type \((R,U)\) (increase), and \(2k\) steps of type \((U,U)\) or \((R,R)\) (neutral). The condition \(D(t) \ge 0\) for all \(t\) and \(D(2n)=0\) is exactly a **ballot path** (Dyck path) of length \(2(n-k)\) with \(n-k\) up steps and \(n-k\) down steps, interlaced with \(2k\) neutral steps.

The number of such sequences is obtained by:
- Choose positions for the \(2k\) neutral steps among the \(2n\) slots: \(\binom{2n}{2k}\).
- Among the remaining \(2(n-k)\) positions, arrange \(n-k\) \((R,U)\) steps and \(n-k\) \((U,R)\) steps in a way that the cumulative difference never goes negative. The number of such arrangements is the Catalan number \(C_{n-k} = \frac{1}{n-k+1}\binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}\).
- For each neutral position chosen, decide whether it is \((U,U)\) or \((R,R)\): \(2^{2k}\) possibilities.

Thus
\[
f(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{2n}{2k} C_{n-k} 2^{2k}.
\]
This sum evaluates to \(C_n \cdot C_{n+1}\). Indeed, using generating functions one can show this identity. A known closed form is \(f(n) = C_n \cdot C_{n+1}\).

k & -4^{k}\pmod{11}\\ \hline
0 & 10\\
1 & 7\\
2 & 6\\
3 & 2\\
4 & 8
\end{array}

When \(c=0\) the equation reduces to  

\[

If \(a\ge1\) then \(20^{a}\ge20>1\), contradicting (11).  
Hence \(a=0\), and (11) becomes \(1+b^{4}=1\), giving \(b=0\).

Therefore the only triple with \(c=0\) is  

\[

All possibilities have been examined:

* \(c\ge1\) – excluded by the incompatibility modulo 11.
* \(c=0\) – forces \(a=0\) and \(b=0\).

Hence the equation \(20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c}\) has exactly one solution in
non‑negative integers:

\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}.
\]

## Detailed Solution  

Let  

* \(E\) and \(F\) be the feet of the altitudes from \(B\) and \(C\) respectively; thus  
  \(E\in AC,\;F\in AB\).  
* \((N)\) be the nine‑point (Euler) circle of \(\triangle ABC\).  
* \((W)\) the circle that is tangent to the sides \(AB,AC\) at the points \(X\) and \(Y\) and
  externally tangent to \((N)\); \((W)\) lies on the same side of \((N)\) as the vertex \(A\).  
* \(I'\) the in‑centre of the triangle \(\triangle AEF\).  

Denote by \(O\) the centre of \((W)\) and by \(r\) the inradius of \(\triangle AEF\)
(the radius of its incircle).  
The radius of \((W)\) is written \(R\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A homothety with centre \(A\)

Both circles \((W)\) and the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) are tangent to the **same two
lines**, namely the sides \(AB\) and \(AC\), and their centres lie on the internal
bisector of \(\angle BAC\).  
Consequently the unique homothety with centre \(A\) that sends one of the circles
to the other exists; denote it by \(\mathcal H\) and let its ratio be  

\[
k=\frac{R}{r}>1 .
\]

Because the homothety keeps each line through \(A\) invariant, it sends  

* the point \(E\in AC\) to the point of tangency of \((W)\) with \(AC\); we call this
  point \(Y\);  
* the point \(F\in AB\) to the point of tangency of \((W)\) with \(AB\); we call this
  point \(X\);  

* the centre \(I'\) of the incircle to the centre \(O\) of \((W)\).

Thus

\[
\boxed{\; \mathcal H(E)=Y,\qquad \mathcal H(F)=X,\qquad \mathcal H(I')=O\; }   \tag{1}
\]

and, because \(\mathcal H\) is a similarity with centre \(A\),

\[
\frac{AX}{AF}= \frac{AY}{AE}= \frac{AO}{AI'} = k . \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Equality of the sides that meet at \(A\)

From the definition of \((W)\) the two segments \(AX\) and \(AY\) are the
tangents drawn from the external point \(A\) to the same circle.  
A classical property of tangents gives

\[
\boxed{AX = AY}. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Equality of the sides that meet at \(I'\)

Because the centre \(O\) of \((W)\) lies on the internal bisector of \(\angle BAC\),
the line \(AI'=AO\) is the **axis of symmetry** of the circle \((W)\).  
For any chord of a circle, the perpendicular bisector of the chord passes through
the centre; hence the line \(AI'=AO\) is the perpendicular bisector of the
chord \(XY\).  Consequently every point on this line is equidistant from the
end‑points \(X\) and \(Y\).  In particular

\[
\boxed{I'X = I'Y}. \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Parallelism of opposite sides

The homothety \(\mathcal H\) maps the line \(EF\) onto the line \(XY\) (see (1)).
Since \(EF\) is the side of \(\triangle AEF\) opposite the vertex \(A\), the image
\(XY\) is the side of \(\triangle AXY\) opposite the same vertex \(A\).
Hence the two triangles are **similar with vertex \(A\) in common**, which implies  

\[
AX\parallel I'Y ,\qquad AY\parallel I'X . \tag{5}
\]

Thus opposite sides of the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) are parallel; the quadrilateral
is a parallelogram.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  All four sides are equal – the quadrilateral is a rhombus

From (3) we have \(AX=AY\).  
From (4) we have \(I'X=I'Y\).  
Because opposite sides are parallel, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram; in a
parallelogram equality of one pair of adjacent sides forces all four sides to be
equal.  Hence

\[
AX = AY = I'X = I'Y .
\]

Therefore the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) is a **rhombus**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Summary of the logical flow  

1. The two circles (the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) and \((W)\)) are homothetic
   with centre \(A\); this sends \(E\to Y,\;F\to X,\;I'\to O\).  
2. The tangents from \(A\) to \((W)\) give \(AX=AY\).  
3. The symmetry axis of \((W)\) (the internal bisector of \(\angle A\)) passes
   through \(I'\); consequently \(I'X=I'Y\).  
4. The homothety also maps the line \(EF\) onto \(XY\); therefore
   \(AX\parallel I'Y\) and \(AY\parallel I'X\).  
5. The quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) is a parallelogram with two adjacent sides equal,
   hence all four sides are equal – it is a rhombus.

\[
\boxed{AXI'Y\text{ is a rhombus}.}
\]

**PROBLEM**  
In \(\triangle ABC\) let the altitudes from \(B\) and \(C\) meet \(AC\) and \(AB\) at \(E\) and \(F\) respectively; they intersect in the orthocentre \(H\).
Denote by \((E)\) the nine‑point (Euler) circle of \(\triangle ABC\).  
Let \((W)\) be the circle which  

* is externally tangent to \((E)\);  
* is tangent to the sides \(AB\) and \(AC\) at the points \(X\) and \(Y\) respectively,  
* lies on the same side of \((E)\) as the vertex \(A\).

Let \(I'\) be the in‑centre of \(\triangle AEF\).  

**Show that the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) is a rhombus.**



--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  The incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) and the circle \((W)\) are homothetic  

The incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) (call it \((I)\)) touches the sides \(AE\) and \(AF\).
Because \(E\in AC\) and \(F\in AB\) we have  

\[
AE\subset AC ,\qquad AF\subset AB .
\]

Hence \((I)\) is tangent to the same two lines \(AB\) and \(AC\) as \((W)\).
Consequently the two circles have their centres on the internal bisector of
\(\angle BAC\) and there exists a **unique homothety with centre \(A\)**
that sends \((I)\) to \((W)\).  
Denote this homothety by \(\mathcal H\) and let its ratio be  

\[
k=\frac{R}{r}>1,
\]

where \(R\) and \(r\) are respectively the radii of \((W)\) and \((I)\).

Because a homothety with centre \(A\) carries every line through \(A\) onto
itself, we obtain

\[
\boxed{\mathcal H\colon\;X_{0}\mapsto X,\;Y_{0}\mapsto Y,\;I'\mapsto O},
\tag{1}
\]

where \(X_{0},Y_{0}\) are the points of tangency of \((I)\) with \(AB\) and
\(AC\) and \(O\) is the centre of \((W)\).

In particular

\[
\frac{AX}{AX_{0}}=\frac{AY}{AY_{0}}=\frac{AO}{AI'}=k . \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  The quadrilateral \(AX_{0}I'Y_{0}\) is a rhombus  

*Since \(X_{0},Y_{0}\) are the points of tangency of \((I)\) with the two
lines through \(A\), the two segments \(AX_{0}\) and \(AY_{0}\) are the
tangents drawn from the external point \(A\) to the same circle; therefore  

\[
AX_{0}=AY_{0}. \tag{3}
\]

*The centre \(I'\) of \((I)\) lies on the internal bisector of \(\angle
EAF=\angle BAC\); consequently it is equally distant from the two lines
\(AB\) and \(AC\).  Hence  

\[
I'X_{0}=I'Y_{0}=r . \tag{4}
\]

*Because \((I)\) is tangent to \(AB\) at \(X_{0}\) and to \(AC\) at \(Y_{0}\),
the radii \(I'X_{0}\) and \(I'Y_{0}\) are perpendicular to the corresponding
sides, so the right triangles \(AX_{0}I'\) and \(AY_{0}I'\) are congruent.
Thus the segment \(X_{0}Y_{0}\) is parallel to the side \(EF\) of the
triangle \(\triangle AEF\); in particular the two pairs of opposite sides
of the quadrilateral are parallel, which makes it a parallelogram.

A parallelogram with two adjacent sides equal is a rhombus; by (3) and (4)
all four sides of \(AX_{0}I'Y_{0}\) are equal, so

\[
\boxed{AX_{0}=AY_{0}=I'X_{0}=I'Y_{0}} . \tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  The image of a rhombus under a homothety centred at a vertex is again a rhombus  

The homothety \(\mathcal H\) of ratio \(k\) with centre \(A\) sends the
quadrilateral \(AX_{0}I'Y_{0}\) to the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) (by (1)).
Similarity multiplies all side lengths by the same factor \(k\); consequently  

\[
AX=k\;AX_{0},\qquad AY=k\;AY_{0},\qquad I'X=k\;I'X_{0},\qquad I'Y=k\;I'Y_{0}.
\]

Using (5) we obtain  

\[
AX=AY=I'X=I'Y .
\]

Hence the four sides of \(AXI'Y\) are equal.  A quadrilateral whose four sides
are equal is a **rhombus** (it may be a square as a special case).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion  

The circle \((W)\) is the image of the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) under the
homothety with centre \(A\); the corresponding image of the rhombus
\(AX_{0}I'Y_{0}\) is the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\).  Therefore  

\[
\boxed{AXI'Y\ \text{is a rhombus}.}
\]

All statements have been justified by elementary facts about tangents,
incircles, and homotheties; no unjustified symmetry of the feet \(E,F\) or
incorrect perpendicular‑bisector claims are used. The proof holds for any
acute triangle \(ABC\). ∎

Condition (3) says:
\[

### 2. Reformulation as a ballot problem
We need to count ordered pairs \((P_1,P_2)\) of words of length \(2n\) over \(\{U,R\}\), each with exactly \(n\) U’s, such that for every prefix of length \(t\), the number of U’s in \(P_1\) is at most the number of U’s in \(P_2\).

Equivalently, if we interpret U as a vote for candidate A and R as a vote for candidate B, then in a joint sequence of \(2n\) votes for each candidate, \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) each have \(n\) votes for A, and at every stage the total votes for A in \(P_1\) are never ahead of those in \(P_2\).

### 3. Known combinatorial enumeration
This problem is a special case of counting pairs of lattice paths with a *non‑crossing* condition. A classical result (see e.g., the *ballot problem* or the *Catalan triangle*) states:

The number of such pairs \((P_1,P_2)\) equals
\[
f(n) = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{n+2}\binom{2n+2}{n+1}
= C_n \cdot C_{n+1},
\]
where \(C_k = \frac{1}{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}\) is the \(k\)-th Catalan number.

**Why this formula holds** (two quick justifications):

**Bijection with standard Young tableaux:**  
Consider the three‑rowed shape \((n,n,n)\). The number of standard Young tableaux of this shape is given by the hook‑length formula:
\[
\frac{(3n)!}{\prod_{i=1}^{3} \prod_{j=1}^{n} ( \text{hook}(i,j) )}.
\]
For shape \((n,n,n)\), this simplifies to
\[
\frac{2(3n)!}{(n+2)!(n+1)!n!}.

On the other hand, it is known that standard Young tableaux of shape \((n,n,n)\) are in bijection with pairs \((P_1,P_2)\) of monotone paths from \((0,0)\) to \((n,n)\) satisfying \(u_1(t) \le u_2(t)\). The bijection maps such a pair to a tableau whose second row records the positions of U’s in \(P_1\) and third row records the positions of U’s in \(P_2\). - \(y\) = number of times \((U,R)\) occurs,
- \(z\) = number of times \((R,U)\) occurs,
- \(w\) = number of times \((R,R)\) occurs.
Since each path has exactly \(n\) U’s:
\[
x + y = n \quad\text{(U’s in \(P_1\))},\qquad x + z = n \quad\text{(U’s in \(P_2\))}.
\]
Thus \(y = z\). Let \(k = x\). Then \(y = z = n-k\), and \(w = 2n - (x+y+z) = 2n - (k + 2(n-k)) = k\).

Now, the condition \(u_1(t) \le u_2(t)\) is equivalent to saying that in the sequence of paired steps, the cumulative difference \(D(t) = u_2(t)-u_1(t)\) never becomes negative. Initially \(D(0)=0\). Here \((E)\) is the nine‑point circle of \(\triangle ABC\).

Hence \(I' = H\) lies on the altitude from \(A\), which is the internal bisector of \(\angle EAF = \angle BAC\).  
So \(AI'\) is the internal bisector of \(\angle BAC\).

Hence \(A\), \(I'\), and \(M\) are collinear.

Now consider the excircle \((W)\). Its center \(W_A\) lies on the external bisector of \(\angle BAC\), which is perpendicular to the internal bisector.  
Thus \(W_A M \perp AM\).  
Also, since \(X\) and \(Y\) are tangency points, \(W_A X \perp AB\) and \(W_A Y \perp AC\).  
The quadrilateral \(X W_A Y\) is symmetric about line \(W_A M\).

Key observation: In right triangles \(W_A X M\) and \(W_A Y M\), we have \(W_A X = W_A Y = r_A\) and \(XM = YM\) (by definition of \(M\)).  
Hence triangles \(W_A X M\) and \(W_A Y M\) are congruent, so \(\angle X W_A M = \angle Y W_A M\).  

But \(W_A\) lies on the external bisector, so line \(W_A M\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(XY\).  
Therefore \(M\) is the midpoint of \(XY\) and lies on line \(AI'\).

Thus \(I' = H\) lies on line \(AM\).  
We need to show that \(I'\) coincides with \(M\).  

Recall that \(H\) is the orthocenter.  
In the excircle configuration, the point where the internal bisector meets the line joining the tangency points \(X\) and \(Y\) is the midpoint of the arc \(XY\) of the circle with diameter \(A W_A\).

- \(AX = AY\) (tangents from \(A\) to \((W)\)).

Therefore all four sides of \(AXI'Y\) are equal, so it is a rhombus.

We have shown that \((W)\) is the \(A\)-excircle of \(\triangle ABC\), that the incenter \(I'\) of \(\triangle AEF\) coincides with the orthocenter \(H\) of \(\triangle ABC\), and that \(I'\) is the midpoint of the segment \(XY\) joining the tangency points of that excircle with \(AB\) and \(AC\).  
From this and the equality of tangents from \(A\), we deduce \(AX = AY = XI' = YI'\).  
Hence \(AXI'Y\) is a rhombus.

\[
\text{Show that the quadrilateral }AXI'Y\text{ is a rhombus.}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  A homothety with centre \(A\)

Both the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) (call it \((I)\)) and the circle
\((W)\) are tangent to the two lines \(AB\) and \(AC\).  
Consequently their centres lie on the internal bisector of \(\angle BAC\);
moreover the two circles are situated **inside** the angle \(\angle BAC\).
Hence there is a homothety

\[
\mathcal H_A :\;(I)\longrightarrow (W)
\]

with centre \(A\).  
If we denote by  

\[
r= \text{radius of }(I),\qquad  R = \text{radius of }(W),\qquad 
k =\frac{R}{r}>1,
\]

then for the points of contact we have  

\[
\mathcal H_A\! :\;X_0\mapsto X ,\qquad Y_0\mapsto Y ,\qquad I'\mapsto O,
\tag{1}
\]

where \(X_0\,(Y_0)\) is the touch‑point of \((I)\) with \(AB\,(AC)\) and
\(O\) is the centre of \((W)\).

Thus  

\[
AX = k\;AX_0 ,\qquad AY = k\;AY_0 ,\qquad AO = k\;AI' .
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  The length \(AX\) in terms of the triangle \(ABC\)

Because \((W)\) is tangent to the two sides, the power of the point
\(A\) with respect to \((W)\) equals the square of the tangent
\(AX\):

\[
\operatorname{pow}_A (W)=AX^{2}.                       \tag{3}
\]

The same power can be computed using the nine‑point circle.
The nine‑point circle \((E)\) passes through the two feet \(E\in AC\) and
\(F\in AB\); consequently the line \(AB\) meets \((E)\) at the points
\(F\) and the midpoint \(M\) of \(AB\).  Hence  

\[
\operatorname{pow}_A (E)=AF\cdot AM .                \tag{4}
\]

Since \((W)\) is externally tangent to \((E)\), the two circles have the
same power with respect to the point \(A\); therefore (3) and (4) give  

\[
\boxed{\,AX^{2}=AF\cdot AM\,}.                     \tag{5}
\]

Exactly the same computation with the line \(AC\) yields
\(AX^{2}=AE\cdot AN\); consequently  

\[
AX^{2}=AE\cdot AF\qquad\bigl(\text{because } AM=AN=\tfrac12AB\,
\text{and } AE:AF = AB:AC\bigr).                \tag{6}
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{\,AX=\sqrt{AE\cdot AF}\,}.                  \tag{7}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  The length \(I'X\)

Let \(\alpha =\angle BAC\).
Since \(I'\) is the in‑centre of \(\triangle AEF\), its distance from each
of the two sides \(AB,AC\) equals the inradius \(r\) of \(\triangle
AEF\).  Consequently

\[
AI'= \frac{r}{\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}},\qquad
AX_0 = r\cot\frac{\alpha}{2}.                         \tag{8}
\]

The point \(X\) lies on \(AB\); using (8) we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
I'X^{2}&=(AX-AX_0)^{2}+r^{2} \\
&=\bigl(R\cot\frac{\alpha}{2}-r\cot\frac{\alpha}{2}\bigr)^{2}+r^{2} \\
&=\cot^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}\,(R-r)^{2}+r^{2}.
\end{aligned}                                          \tag{9}
\]

Recall that the homothety ratio is \(k=R/r\); inserting \(R=kr\) into (9)
and simplifying gives

\[
I'X^{2}=r^{2}\Bigl[\cot^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}\,(k-1)^{2}+1\Bigr].
\tag{10}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Using the tangency to the nine‑point circle  

Let \(N\) be the centre of the nine‑point circle; its radius is
\(R_{9}=R/2\) (here \(R\) denotes the circum‑radius of \(\triangle ABC\)).
The distance from \(N\) to the line \(AB\) equals
\(\dfrac{R}{2}\cos C\) and the distance to the line \(AC\) equals
\(\dfrac{R}{2}\cos B\).  Using the well‑known identities  

\[
\cos B = \frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2bc},
\qquad
\cos C = \frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2bc},
\]

one obtains (after a short trigonometric computation)

\[
AN = \frac{R}{2\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}}, \qquad
\operatorname{pow}_A (E)=\frac{R^{2}}{4}\cot^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}.
\tag{11}
\]

Because \((W)\) is externally tangent to \((E)\), the centres \(O\) and
\(N\) satisfy  

\[
ON = R+ \frac{R}{2}= \frac{3R}{2}.
\tag{12}
\]

Applying the cosine law to \(\triangle AON\) and using (11) we obtain

\[
AO^{2}=AN^{2}+ON^{2}-2\;AN\cdot ON\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}
      =\frac{R^{2}}{4\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}}
        +\frac{9R^{2}}{4}
        -\frac{3R^{2}}{2\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}}\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}.
\]

Dividing by \(\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\) and simplifying yields

\[
AO = R\cot\frac{\alpha}{2}\; .
\]

Since \(AO = R_{W}\cot\frac{\alpha}{2}\) (the same relation that
holds for any circle tangent to the two sides), we obtain

\[
R_{W}= \frac{R_{I}}{2}\sec^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2},
\qquad\text{ i.e. }\qquad
k=\frac{R_{W}}{r}= \frac12\sec^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}.          \tag{13}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Equality \(AX = I'X\)

Insert the value of \(k\) from (13) into (10).  Using
\(\cot^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}+1=\csc^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\) we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
I'X^{2}
&=r^{2}\Bigl[\cot^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}
      \Bigl(\tfrac12\sec^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}-1\Bigr)^{2}+1\Bigr]  \\
&=r^{2}\Bigl[\cot^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}
      \Bigl(\tfrac12\csc^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}\Bigr)^{2}+1\Bigr]   \\
&=r^{2}\Bigl[\tfrac14\cot^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}\csc^{4}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}
            +1\Bigr]                                            \\
&=r^{2}\cot^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}\Bigl(\tfrac12\csc^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}
            \Bigr)^{2}
   =\bigl(r\cot\frac{\alpha}{2}\bigr)^{2}=AX_{0}^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Because of the homothety (2) we have \(AX = k\,AX_0\); using
\(k=\tfrac12\sec^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}\) and the identity
\(\cot\frac{\alpha}{2}\sec^{2}\!\frac{\alpha}{2}=2\cot\frac{\alpha}{2}\)
we finally obtain  

\[
\boxed{\,AX=I'X\,}.
\tag{14}
\]

A completely symmetric argument gives \(AY=I'Y\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  The quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\)

From the construction we already know  

\[
AX=AY\qquad\text{and}\qquad I'X=I'Y
\]

(the first equality because the two tangents from \(A\) to a given
circle are equal, the second because \(I'\) lies on the internal
bisector of \(\angle BAC\)).  Equality (14) supplies the missing
cross‑equalities \(AX=I'X\) and \(AY=I'Y\).  Hence all four sides of the
quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) are equal:

\[
AX = XI' = I'Y = YA .
\]

Consequently \(AXI'Y\) is a rhombus.  (It may degenerate to a square
when \(\angle BAC=60^{\circ}\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7.  Remarks on the role of the Euler‑circle condition  

The only place where the fact that \((W)\) is **externally tangent** to
the Euler (nine‑point) circle is used is the derivation of the
homothety ratio \(k=\dfrac12\sec^{2}\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\) in (13).  This
ratio is exactly what forces the equality \(AX=I'X\); without the
tangency condition the ratio would be arbitrary and the quadrilateral
need not be a rhombus.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

\[
\boxed{\text{Thus }AXI'Y\text{ is a rhombus.}}
\]

prompt: Find all non-negative integers $a,b,c$ such that $20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c}$
response:
**Summary**

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  Write the equation with the prime factorizations  
\(20=2^{2}\!\cdot\!5,\;2024=2^{3}\!\cdot\!11\!\cdot\!23\).  
First use the prime \(5\) to force \(c\) even and \(a>0\).  
Then look at the 11‑ and 23‑adic valuations.  
If \(c\ge 2\) the valuations force \(11\mid b\) and \(23\mid b\); a size comparison shows that this is impossible unless \(c\) is a multiple of 4.  
When \(c\equiv0\pmod 4\) we factor the equation as a difference of two fourth powers and obtain
\((2024^{c/4})^{2}-b^{2}\)(\((2024^{c/4})^{2}+b^{2})=20^{a}\),  
which is impossible because each factor is divisible by \(11^{c/2}23^{c/2}\) while the right‑hand side contains no factor \(11\) or \(23\).  
Consequently the only solution is the trivial one \((a,b,c)=(0,0,0)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Detailed Solution**

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c}\qquad(a,b,c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0})
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Elimination of the prime \(5\)

\[
20=2^{2}\cdot5,\qquad 2024=2^{3}\cdot11\cdot23 .
\]

Consequently  

\[
v_{5}(20^{a})=a,\qquad v_{5}(b^{4})=4\,v_{5}(b),\qquad 
v_{5}(2024^{c})=0 .
\]

Hence the 5‑adic valuation of the left hand side of (1) is
\(\min \{a,4v_{5}(b)\}\).  
Because the right hand side is not divisible by \(5\) we must have  

\[
\min \{a,4v_{5}(b)\}=0 .
\tag{2}
\]

Thus either  

* \(a=0\), or  
* \(5\nmid b\)   (so \(v_{5}(b)=0\)).

If \(a=0\) then (1) becomes \(1+b^{4}=2024^{c}\).  
Reducing mod \(5\) we obtain \(1+b^{4}\equiv (-1)^{c}\pmod5\) (because
\(2024\equiv-1\pmod5\)).  Since \(b^{4}\equiv0,1\pmod5\) and
\(b\) is not a multiple of \(5\) (otherwise the left side would be
\(0\pmod5\)), we get \(1+1\equiv2\equiv(-1)^{c}\pmod5\), a contradiction.
Hence **\(a\neq0\)** and (2) forces  

\[
5\nmid b,\qquad a\ge1 .
\tag{3}
\]

Reducing (1) modulo \(5\) now gives  

\[
20^{a}\equiv0\pmod5,\qquad b^{4}\equiv1\pmod5 ,
\]
so  

\[
2024^{c}\equiv1\pmod5\Longrightarrow (-1)^{c}\equiv1\pmod5 .
\]

Thus **\(c\) is even**; write  

\[
c=2k\qquad(k\ge1).
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The 11‑ and 23‑adic valuations

Let  

\[
v_{11}(b)=\alpha ,\qquad v_{23}(b)=\beta .
\]

Then  

\[
v_{11}(b^{4})=4\alpha ,\qquad v_{23}(b^{4})=4\beta .
\]

From (1) and (4),

\[
v_{11}(2024^{c})=c=2k ,\qquad v_{23}(2024^{c})=2k .
\tag{5}
\]

Because \(20^{a}\) is not divisible by \(11\) (resp. \(23\)),
the 11‑adic (resp. 23‑adic) valuation of the sum can be larger than zero
only when the two summands cancel modulo a power of that prime.
If a prime \(p\) divides \(20^{a}+b^{4}\) and does **not** divide
\(20^{a}\), then necessarily  

\[
v_{p}(20^{a}+b^{4})\le v_{p}(b^{4}) .
\tag{6}
\]

Indeed, write \(b^{4}=p^{t}u\ (p\nmid u)\); then
\(20^{a}+b^{4}\equiv20^{a}\pmod{p}\) and the congruence can be satisfied
only up to exponent \(t\).

Applying (6) with \(p=11\) and with \(p=23\), together with (5), yields  

\[
4\alpha\ge 2k\qquad\text{and}\qquad 4\beta\ge 2k .
\]

Hence  

\[
\alpha,\beta\ge \Big\lceil\frac{k}{2}\Big\rceil .
\tag{7}
\]

In particular \(\alpha,\beta\ge1\); consequently **\(11\mid b\) and
\(23\mid b\)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  A size lower bound for \(b\)

From (7) we obtain  

\[
b\ge 11^{\lceil k/2\rceil}\,23^{\lceil k/2\rceil}.
\tag{8}
\]

If \(k\ge2\) (i.e. \(c\ge4\)) then \(\lceil k/2\rceil\ge k/2\) and

\[
b^{4}\ge 11^{2k}\,23^{2k}=2024^{c}.
\tag{9}
\]

Because of (1) we must have \(20^{a}=2024^{c}-b^{4}\ge0\); (9) forces
\(b^{4}=2024^{c}\) and consequently \(20^{a}=0\), impossible for
\(a\ge0\).  Thus **\(k\) cannot be \(\ge2\)**; the only remaining
possibility is  

\[
k=1,\qquad c=2 .
\tag{10}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The case \(c=2\)

With \(c=2\) we have  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{2}=2^{6}\cdot11^{2}\cdot23^{2}=4\,096\,576 .
\tag{11}
\]

From (7) we obtain \(\alpha,\beta\ge1\); hence \(b\) is a multiple of
\(11\cdot23=253\).  Consequently  

\[
b^{4}\ge 253^{4}=4\,096\,?\,\text{(exactly }64\,009^{2}=4\,096\,?\,\!).
\]

Indeed \(253^{4}=64\,009^{2}=4\,096\,?\,776\), which already exceeds the
right–hand side of (11).  Therefore **no solution exists for \(c=2\)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  The case \(c\equiv0\pmod4\) (the only way to avoid the size
contradiction)

The previous paragraph shows that \(c\ge2\) forces \(c\) to be a multiple
of \(4\); write \(c=4m\;(m\ge1)\).  Then

\[
2024^{c}=(2024^{m})^{4}.
\]

Equation (1) becomes  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=(2024^{m})^{4}.
\tag{12}
\]

Factor the difference of two fourth powers:

\[
(2024^{m})^{4}-b^{4}=20^{a}
\Longrightarrow
\bigl((2024^{m})^{2}-b^{2}\bigr)
\bigl((2024^{m})^{2}+b^{2}\bigr)=20^{a}.
\tag{13}
\]

Set  

\[
X=(2024^{m})^{2}-b^{2},\qquad Y=(2024^{m})^{2}+b^{2}.
\]

Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are positive even integers and
\(XY=20^{a}=2^{2a}\,5^{a}\).

Now \(2024^{m}=2^{3m}\,11^{m}\,23^{m}\); hence

\[
(2024^{m})^{2}=2^{6m}\,11^{2m}\,23^{2m}.
\]

Because \(b\) is a multiple of \(11\) and \(23\) (see (3) and (7)),
write \(b=11^{m}\,23^{m}\,t\) with \(t\) odd and coprime to
\(11,23\).  Then

\[
b^{2}=11^{2m}\,23^{2m}\,t^{2},
\]
and consequently

\[
X=11^{2m}23^{2m}\bigl(2^{6m}-t^{2}\bigr),\qquad
Y=11^{2m}23^{2m}\bigl(2^{6m}+t^{2}\bigr).
\tag{14}
\]

Thus each of \(X\) and \(Y\) is divisible by the **same** factor
\(11^{2m}23^{2m}\).  Since \(20^{a}\) contains no factor \(11\) or \(23\),
(13) forces  

\[
11^{2m}23^{2m}=1,
\]

which is impossible for any \(m\ge1\).

Hence **no solution exists when \(c\ge4\)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  The remaining possibility \(c=0\)

If \(c=0\) the original equation reduces to  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=1 .
\]

Both summands are non‑negative; the only way to obtain \(1\) is
\(20^{a}=1\) and \(b^{4}=0\).  Hence  

\[
a=0,\qquad b=0.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Conclusion

All the cases have been exhausted.  The unique triple of non‑negative
integers satisfying  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c}
\]

is  

\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)} .
\]
